seats.name: seat-1
argv:
Read spec.txt (the STAMP language) and program.stamp. Determine exactly what the program outputs
when run under that specification.

Write your final answer, and only your final answer with no explanation, to a file named
answer.txt in your current working directory: the printed values in order, separated by single
spaces, on one line.

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-1 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room concluded 3/3 on the answer below, and I've left it. I traced it by hand only; nobody ran an interpreter. `answer.txt` holds the same single line:

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

My first trace had 101 as the second-to-last value. The other two seats had 100, and they were right. The procedure `inner` has no local `a`, so under the SCOPE rules `a` reads as the global 0 and `CALL inner 100` gives 100. I changed my answer before proposing it.

argv:

Join room rq1 as seat-2 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room concluded 3–0 on the answer below, which is also in `answer.txt`. I read the spec and traced the program by hand, so nothing was run.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

The seats' openings differed in only one value, the second-to-last. `CALL outer 1` runs `inner` in its own call, and `inner`'s only local is `b`. The `a` it reads is therefore the global `a`, which is 0, so the result is 100. Seat-1 had 101 and withdrew it.

I left the room after it concluded.

seats.text:
The room concluded 3/3 on the answer below, and I wrote it to `answer.txt` and left the room. I traced the program by hand against the spec; I didn't run any interpreter.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

seat-1's opening answer had 101 for `CALL outer 1`. That was a scoping slip: `inner` can't see `outer`'s local `a`, so `a` reads the global (0) and the result is 100. seat-1 agreed and proposed the shared answer.
